name: The Taichu calendrical system of Han China
summary: In 104 BCE the Han court adopted a reformed official calendar, the Taichu system, which fixed the year's start at the first month and stayed in use until 85 CE.
description: In 104 BCE Emperor Wu of Han replaced the calendar inherited from Qin with a system worked out under the astronomers Deng Ping and Luoxia Hong, named Taichu after the reign period that began that year. It fixed the beginning of the year at the first month and placed intercalary months by the solar terms. The sources also credit it with synodic periods for the planets and a 135-month eclipse cycle, constants that are known through a later version of the system. It is the oldest Chinese calendar whose data are fully recorded, and it stayed in use until 85 CE.

impact.note: The official calendar ordered the year for most of Chinese society, and its year beginning lasted (reach 2); it reformed a calendar that already existed (depth 1); later Han systems revised it (generativity 1).

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Find a dated scholarly source (for example Cullen) for Liu Xin's Santong system and whether the planetary and eclipse constants belong to the Taichu system of 104 BCE or to that revision.
Source the Mawangdui planetary text of 168 BCE as earlier evidence of planetary computation.

Settle the dates of Luoxia Hong: MacTutor gives about 130 to 70 BCE, and the 156-87 printed after his name in the ChinaKnowledge quotation matches Emperor Wu's lifetime and may be misattributed there.
Replace the two tertiary sources with a history of Chinese astronomy that cites the Han shu and Shiji.

research.note: The sources describe a Han court reform of an existing Chinese calendar; none says whether its planetary and eclipse methods were reached without knowledge of western Asian astronomy.
